title: 31. Array Methods: pop, shift, and unshift
theory:
Beyond push() which adds to the end, JavaScript provides three more essential methods for manipulating the elements of an array at its boundaries.

pop()

Removes the last element from an array. It also returns that removed element in case you want to save it in a variable.

shift()

Removes the first element from an array (at index 0). All other elements are shifted down by one index.

unshift()

Adds one or more elements to the beginning of an array. All other elements are shifted up.
output:
> Original: [10, 20, 30]
> After pop: [10, 20]
> After unshift: [5, 10, 20]
> After shift: [10, 20]

title: 32. Iterating Arrays with For Loops
theory:
Arrays and Loops are best friends in programming. An array holds a list of data, and a loop allows you to automatically execute code for every single piece of data in that list.

We can use a standard for loop to iterate over an array. The trick is to start the loop counter i at 0 (since arrays are zero-indexed), and set the condition to run as long as i is less than the array's length.

Inside the loop, we use array[i] to dynamically access the current element as the loop progresses.
output:
> Processing item: Apple
> Processing item: Banana
> Processing item: Cherry

title: 33. Introduction to Objects
theory:
Arrays are great for ordered lists, but they are terrible if you want to store complex, structured data where each piece of information has a specific label. For this, we use Objects.

An Object is a collection of Key-Value pairs. It is declared using curly braces {}.

Keys and Values

The Key (also called a Property name) acts as a label. The Value is the data associated with that label. Values can be anything: Strings, Numbers, Arrays, or even other Objects!

Objects are the most important data structure in JavaScript. They allow us to group related data together logically (e.g., storing a User's name, email, and age in one place).

title: 34. Modifying Objects
theory:
Just like Arrays, Objects are mutable. You can easily add new properties, update existing properties, or even delete properties entirely after the object has been created.

Dot Notation vs Bracket Notation

You can modify objects using standard Dot Notation (e.g., user.age = 31). However, if your Key has a space in it, or if you are using a variable to dynamically select a Key, you must use Bracket Notation (e.g., user['age'] = 31).
output:
> Original Age: 30
> Updated Age: 31
> Added City: New York

title: 35. Object Methods
theory:
Objects don't just store static data (like strings and numbers). They can also store Functions! When a function is stored inside an object as a property, we call it a Method.

Methods allow objects to have behaviors. For example, a 'User' object might have a 'login' method, or a 'Car' object might have a 'drive' method.

The 'this' Keyword

Inside an object method, the keyword this acts as a reference to the object itself. It allows the method to access other properties belonging to the same object (e.g., this.name).
output:
> Engine started. Vroom!
> The Toyota is driving.

title: 36. Introduction to the DOM
theory:
JavaScript was created to make web pages interactive. But how does JavaScript actually talk to the HTML? Through the DOM (Document Object Model).

When a web browser loads an HTML file, it translates all the HTML tags (like <h1>, <div>, <p>) into a massive JavaScript Object. This structured object tree is the DOM.

The Document Object

The entry point to the DOM is a globally available object called document. By using the document object in JavaScript, we can read the page structure, change text, change colors, or add completely new elements dynamically!
output:
> [Digital Console Representation]
> Accessing the DOM...
> document.title holds the page title.

title: 37. Selecting DOM Elements
theory:
Before we can change a heading or a button on our webpage, we must first tell JavaScript which element we want to modify. We do this by "selecting" elements from the DOM.

Methods for Selecting:

  • getElementById(): Finds a single element by its unique HTML id attribute.
  • querySelector(): The most modern and powerful method. It uses CSS selectors (like .class or #id) to find the first matching element.
  • querySelectorAll(): Finds ALL elements matching a CSS selector and returns them in a list.
output:
> Selected Heading Element
> Selected Button Element

title: 38. Modifying Text and HTML
theory:
Once we have selected an element from the DOM and stored it in a variable, we can change its contents. JavaScript provides properties on the element object to do exactly this.

innerText vs innerHTML

innerText: This property allows you to read or replace the raw text inside an element. It is safe and ignores HTML tags.

innerHTML: This property allows you to read or inject actual HTML tags into the element. While powerful, it can be dangerous if used with user-submitted data (Cross-Site Scripting attacks), so use it carefully!
output:
> Old Title Text changed to: 'JavaScript is Awesome!'
> HTML injected into the container.

title: 39. Modifying CSS Styles via JS
theory:
JavaScript can also manipulate the visual design of the page dynamically. There are two primary ways to do this:

1. Inline Styles (element.style)

You can directly apply CSS properties. Note: CSS properties with hyphens (like background-color) are converted to camelCase (backgroundColor) in JavaScript because hyphens signify subtraction in JS.

2. Class List (element.classList)

The better and cleaner approach is to have pre-defined CSS classes in your stylesheet, and use JavaScript to simply add(), remove(), or toggle() those classes on an element.
output:
> Styles updated successfully.
> Box is now Blue and has 'active' class.

title: 40. Introduction to Events
theory:
A static webpage is boring. Interactivity requires the page to respond to the user. An Event is any action that happens in the browser—a mouse click, a key press, scrolling, or submitting a form.

Event Listeners

To make our JavaScript react to these events, we use a method called addEventListener(). We attach it to a DOM element, tell it what specific event to listen for (like 'click'), and give it a Function to execute whenever that event happens.

This is the core foundation of all interactive web applications!
output:
> System standing by...
> (When user clicks the button)
> Button was clicked! Executing code...
